questions.q: What does FOR JSON AUTO turn a query's results into?
options: A single JSON array with one JSON object per row
A single JSON scalar value
A CSV-formatted string
An XML document
questions.explain: FOR JSON AUTO converts the whole result set into a JSON array, with each row becoming one JSON object.

questions.q: How does FOR JSON AUTO decide where to nest a joined table's columns?
options: It infers the nesting automatically from the table/join shape in the query
It always nests the first table's columns, never the second
It never nests anything — all columns stay flat
It requires an explicit WITH NESTING clause
questions.explain: AUTO infers nested JSON structure based on how the tables are joined, without needing explicit instructions.

questions.q: In FOR JSON PATH, what does a column alias like [Product.Name] produce?
options: An error, because dots aren't allowed in aliases
A JSON array named Product
A flat column literally named 'Product.Name'
A nested JSON object: {"Product": {"Name": ...}}
questions.explain: FOR JSON PATH uses dotted aliases to build explicit nested JSON structure, regardless of the underlying join.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of FOR JSON PATH over FOR JSON AUTO?
options: PATH works without any FROM clause
PATH automatically removes NULL values
PATH is faster to execute than AUTO
PATH gives explicit, direct control over the JSON structure via aliases, instead of relying on inference from the join
questions.explain: PATH lets you dictate the exact nested shape yourself, rather than depending on how SQL Server infers it from the query's join shape.

options: Forces FOR JSON to always return an array, even for zero rows
Converts the output from JSON back into a regular rowset
Removes all nested objects from the JSON output
Removes the default [ ] array wrapper, returning a plain JSON object instead of a one-element array
questions.explain: By default FOR JSON always wraps output in an array; WITHOUT_ARRAY_WRAPPER strips that wrapper for a single-object result.
